title: Leaders Who Hijack Meetings
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article identifies a specific failure mode in otherwise passionate, engaging leaders: a recency bias toward whatever has most recently excited them, which drives them to derail meetings by inserting their own stories and breakthroughs at the expense of the agenda. It notes the leaders doing this genuinely don't realize they're doing damage, since their enthusiasm feels productive to them even as it consumes time meant for other priorities. The piece offers a delicate remedy, since directly telling a leader they're hurting productivity risks a defensive reaction — instead recommending a strong agenda upfront paired with an explicit promise of dedicated time at the end for the leader's stories and insights. It closes by acknowledging passion is genuinely valuable in leadership, just in need of a 'lid' when it overrides what a meeting actually needs to accomplish.
points: A recency bias toward whatever most recently excited them drives some passionate leaders to unconsciously derail meeting agendas with their own stories.
Leaders exhibiting this pattern usually don't realize the harm, since their enthusiasm feels productive from the inside.
Direct feedback about the pattern risks a defensive reaction, so a strong upfront agenda plus an explicit promise of dedicated time at the end is recommended instead.
The piece frames the fix as putting a 'lid' on genuinely valuable passion, not eliminating it.
quotes: It’s common for high-energy and passionate storytellers to have a recency bias. They want to tell others about whatever has most excited them lately.
Unknowingly, they take conversations and discussions off track by introducing their most recent breakthrough from the first moment in a meeting.
Many leaders with this weakness often don’t realize they do this and generally can’t stop themselves, even when they are aware.
The better choice is to set a strong and clear agenda and then to remind everyone that there will be time at the end to discuss recent developments and insights.
A leader’s passion to share their insights is a good thing until it overrides what needs to get done and discussed. Then that passion needs a lid.
